I make myself alternate between fiction and non-fiction in an attempt to broaden my reading tastes. I am about to finish the first Mistborn book, which is amazing if you like sci-fi, and now need a new non-fiction to get into. Last one I read was Kitchen Confidential by Anthony Bourdain and a history book before that so I will try anything if it seems interesting.
looking for my next non-fiction book any good suggestions
The Devil's Alliance by Moorhouse makes a good read that goes in depth with the Stalin and Hitler pact. I could recommend more, but I don't know what you're interested in :P

I just mentioned this in another thread, but I'm currently reading Days Of Rage by Bryan Burrough, which is a history of the violent revolutionary movements of the 60s and 70s. It's a fascinating and well-researched story of a time whose violence is really surprising -- and, the author argues, often forgotten. He interviewed a number of former members of these movements who speak out for the first time.

On a totally different track, if your interested in behind-the-scenes stories of moviemaking, I really enjoyed Fiasco: A History of Hollywood's Iconic Flops by James Robert Parish. Parish is a former publicity guy, so he analyzes well-known bombs like Last Action Hero from that perspective. But the best part is that he names names and gives detailed quotes from contemporary media that really explain why a film went wrong, and what really happened. Some of it gets a bit gossipy (He claims someone challenged Clint Eastwood to a duel on the set of Paint Your Wagon, something that wasn't mentioned in an Eastwood biography I read) but much of it is backed up from other sources. Very readable and informative.
I really enjoyed The Peoples History of the United States by Howard Zinn. You don't have to be American to enjoy it either. It's a real perspective-fuck on events in Americas history.
I read this one, it is really great. Learned a lot that I missed in history class.

Lost in Shangri-La by Mitchell Zuckoff. It's a true story about a plane that crashes in Papa New Guinea during WWII, and how the indigenous people there were basically living in stone-age times with no knowledge of the outside world. Pretty interesting.

Killing Lincoln. Some people may have problems with the author's political views, but this is all about Lincoln, no politics involved. I believe he was a history teacher before he became a pundit (O'Reilly, not Lincoln)
I have heard good things about this one, and it was from an anti fox news friend of mine. Might have to give this one a try

Today I went to a dumpling food truck. I asked them if the veggie dumplings had any dairy or eggs and they said no. When I got back to my office I discovered that the vendor, out of the goodness of his heart, gave me 10 dumplings instead of 6 I ordered and I was like 'cool'. I ate 7 dumplings and they had vegetables in them. I bite into the 7th one and lo and behold there's some king of meat in it. I hate wasting food so I just ended up eating it. another example was when out of my sheer stupidity I didn't realize there was honey in the cocktail during a tasting until I was mid-way into drinking it, so I was like 'now I gotta drink the rest'. What do you do in situations like these?
What do you do when you discover food you are eating is not vegan... while eating it?

It's really up to you, and mistakes are mistakes. Personally if realized I was eating something with meat, I would stop eating. I might try to at least give it to someone who will finish it because yea, hate wasting!

It's happened to me a couple times. I've learned to read labels carefully every time because it's almost like a game for psychopaths figuring out ways to get animal products into everything. The last one that got me was planters nuts with their gelatin.

If I'm at a restaurant I'll let the server know I'm vegan, but still spell it out quite clearly by saying no cheese, no butter, no chunks of animal carcass, etc while ordering because a lot of people don't even know what vegan means. If after all that, there's something non-vegan on the plate I'll send it back (unless it's easily separable).

I guess if I were lax about ordering something and didn't specify it'd be different, that's my mistake. Still, I'm not going to eat something non-vegan on purpose. The cheese has already been made, or the animal already killed. It doesn't care if I eat it or not, the damage has been done. It's like the logic in saying clean your plate, there's starving people in the world. Me eating or not doesn't help starving people just like me eating a vegetable wrap smothered in ranch doesn't make a cow feel better about being a cog in the dairy machine.

I so agree with you about reading the labels. Recently found out there was milk in some guac and hummus. That's just sick, man. I understand your argument about me eating cheese not helping the cow. I guess because I'm more of an enviro-vegan than an ethical vegan (or whatever you call a person who does it for the animals) the thought of just throwing stuff out repulses me. I mean I obviously oppose animal slaughter, but that's not the main reason I chose to be vegan.

I usually stop eating the item. I lose my appetite. However, I generally agree with the 99-99.9% rule: try your best, ask questions, but realize that shit happens. Also, I have an omni partner who will eat stuff for me, which takes care of the waste concern. Keep on keepin' on!

I think it depends on the situation and the "type" of vegan you are. You mentioned you were more of an enviro-vegan, and like mmm_sammiches mentioned, mistakes are mistakes.

I can't speak for anyone but myself (obviously), but I would think some folks who are ethical vegans (as I am) would choose not to continuing eating just because they don't want to eat another being, regardless of the situation.

And I understand not wanting to waste food. But the argument of "the animal has already given its life," is kind of a sticky one. If this were the case, and I didn't want an animal to die needlessly, then every time I walked into a grocery store, I would feel the need to buy every animal product there. Of course, that's an extreme exaggeration, but then you can see how that would affect the demand for more animal products.

It also has to do with customer supply and demand. If a restaurant gets an order wrong, I think it's a good idea to let them know and ask for something else. They probably want to know anyway if they are satisfying their customers.

On the other hand, if you order something and take it away, what choice do you have? You could call the place and complain or go back, but that's not always an option, say, if you're traveling.

So yeah, being vegan, trying to suck less, excluding "as far as is possible and practicable" the exploitation of animals, I do my best! ;)

Yeah, I spoke to some non-vegan friends about this situation yesterday and they said that 'the point' of veganism is to not put animal products in your body. I guess that's the general rule. But I really like the "as far as is possible and practicable" part of the definition because sometimes shit just happens.

Stop eating. Take a deep breath. Realize it happened again. The world isn't ending, but you're probably gonna get a sore on your tongue (whenever I eat anything non-organic or non-vegan, or even vegan but bad, i.e. oreo's, I get sores on my tongue). Take a bit of Apple Cider Vinegar and try to do better next time.

Been about 8 years for me, still happens.

You can't un-kill animals and un-harvest their secretions. At the point you discover something you've already gotten isn't vegan, it can be a matter of whether you want to eat it or not for health reasons, assuming that returning the food is not an option. So you can either choose to eat it, or perhaps you can give it to someone else who is not a vegan. The rationale behind giving it away to a non-vegan is that hopefully that's less non-vegan food he/she will buy that day. I don't think it's okay to throw it away, thus wasting it and resulting in you still causing more pollution in meeting your needs that day.
